summary: Details how labels are distributed to and from ATM label switching routers using LDP when routes come from ordinary network-layer routing. It extends and clarifies RFC 3031 and RFC 3036. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: ATM equipment already has its own way of labeling traffic. This explains how to make MPLS use it so both can work together.

questions: how does mpls work over atm
how is ttl handled in mpls over atm
subtitle: How ATM switches can act as MPLS label switching routers, using their VPI/VCI fields as labels.

tldr.problem: ATM switches forward cells by labels in the cell header and cannot do things routers do, such as decrement an IP TTL, so they need special rules to act as MPLS label switching routers.
tldr.mechanism: The label is carried in the VPI/VCI (or VCI) field, labels are handed out by LDP downstream-on-demand, a hop count tracks the path length, and edge routers add a shim header and adjust the TTL on behalf of the switches.
tldr.outcome: ATM switches can run ordinary routing protocols and forward on labels with no ATM-specific routing or addressing. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3035 is a Proposed Standard, published in January 2001, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: ATM Switches as Label Switching Routers
sections.content:
The MPLS architecture (RFC 3031) allows ATM switches to serve as Label Switching Routers. These ATM-LSRs run network layer routing algorithms such as OSPF and IS-IS and forward data based on the results. No ATM-specific routing or addressing is needed.

RFC 3035 extends and clarifies parts of RFC 3031 and the LDP specification (RFC 3036). It covers label distribution for routes chosen hop by hop by ordinary routing, using the technique called downstream-on-demand. Non-merging ATM-LSRs MUST use it; it is OPTIONAL for VC-merge-capable ones. It also defines the encapsulation for labeled packets, and is a companion to RFC 3032.

It does not cover explicitly chosen routes, routes that diverge from conventional hop-by-hop routing, multicast FECs or VP merge.
sections.plainLanguage: Some postal sorting machines already read a tag on each parcel. This document says how to reuse those machines for a newer, smarter tagging system.

sections.title: Key Definitions and ATM Constraints
sections.content:
A label switching controlled ATM (LC-ATM) interface is an ATM interface run by the label switching control component. The top label is inferred from the VCI field, or from the VPI and VCI fields together, and LDP peers negotiate which. An ATM-LSR forwards cells between LC-ATM interfaces using those labels, without reassembling cells into frames. A frame-based LSR forwards complete frames. The frame-based LSRs attached to an ATM-LSR domain form its Edge Set, and are called Edge LSRs.

VC-merge is receiving cells on several incoming VCIs and sending them on one outgoing VCI without interleaving the cells of different AAL5 PDUs.

ATM hardware sets the rules: label swapping happens on the VCI and/or VPI in the cell header, which fixes the size and place of the label. Multipoint-to-point VCs are generally unsupported, so most switches cannot VC-merge, and there is generally no TTL-decrement function. The ATM control component (UNI, PNNI) is not required, and a switch may run it alongside label switching as independent control components ("ships in the night").
sections.plainLanguage: The old machines can only change the tag on a parcel. They cannot count how many stops a parcel made or mix parcels into one belt, so special rules fill the gaps.

sections.title: Using VPI/VCI Values as Labels
sections.content:
In an ATM-LSR the label rides in the VPI/VCI field, or in the VCI field alone when two ATM-LSRs are linked over an ATM Virtual Path. Labeled packets MUST use the null encapsulation of Section 6.1 of RFC 2684.

Peers on an LC-ATM interface MUST also have a non-MPLS connection able to carry unlabeled IP packets. It carries LDP packets, and the LLC/SNAP encapsulation MUST be used on it. Its default value is VPI 0, VCI 32; over a Virtual Path the default VCI is 32. Other values can be configured if both sides know them.

A VPI/VCI whose VCI is in the range 0-32 inclusive MUST NOT be used as a label. Allowed ranges are communicated through LDP, and may differ per VPI. Connections across ATM switched virtual circuits are not specified here; they are handled by RFC 3038 using a VCID.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag is written in the spot on the cell where the ATM address already goes. A few low tag numbers are kept off limits, and one separate channel carries the control chatter.

sections.title: Label Distribution Procedures
sections.content:
With downstream-on-demand distribution, an Edge LSR whose next hop for a FEC is an ATM-LSR asks that neighbor for a label binding, with the hop count in the request set to 1. An ATM-LSR that receives a request allocates a label, requests a binding from its own next hop, and returns the allocated label upstream. The hop count in each request must be one more than in the request it received.

A maximum hop count, MAXHOP, defaults to 255 and may be configured. If a request's hop count would exceed it, the request MUST NOT be sent on and the upstream neighbor is told it cannot be satisfied. An ATM-LSR may wait for the answer from downstream (ordered control) or answer at once with hop count 0, meaning unknown (independent control). A hop count of 0 is passed upstream unchanged.

A non-merging ATM-LSR MUST create a new binding, and a new downstream request, for every request. When a next hop changes, the former next hop is told the binding is no longer needed. A VC-merge-capable ATM-LSR needs only one outgoing label per FEC: if it already has one, it allocates an incoming label and replaces it with the existing outgoing label, without asking downstream again. It still gives each upstream requester its own binding, since upstream switches may not merge. Hop count changes propagate back toward the ingress, and exceeding MAXHOP means bindings are withdrawn, which breaks loops from routing transients.
sections.plainLanguage: Each stop asks the next stop for a tag, one after another down the road. A counter tracks how many stops there are, and if it gets too big, everyone knows something is going in circles.

sections.title: Encapsulation and the Shim Header
sections.content:
Only Edge LSRs deal with encapsulation; the ATM-LSRs never change it. Labeled packets use the null encapsulation, and a packet on an LC-ATM interface MUST also carry a shim header (RFC 3032) with one entry for each entry in its label stack.

The real top label sits in the VPI/VCI field. The top shim entry is only a placeholder: its label value MUST be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on reception. The packet's outgoing TTL and CoS go in the top shim entry's TTL and CoS fields. A packet with a single label still needs a single-entry shim of 4 bytes, so a receiver can always tell whether more label stack entries follow.

The extra overhead can be avoided only by knowing in advance that packets carry one label, or by using two VCs per FEC. The RFC doubts either has practical utility.
sections.plainLanguage: Even when the tag is on the outside of the envelope, a small note is kept inside so the reader can tell whether there are more tags stacked up.

sections.title: TTL Handling and Loop Detection
sections.content:
Since ATM-LSRs cannot decrement TTL, Edge LSRs do it for them. The incoming TTL comes from the IP header of an unlabeled packet, or from the top label stack entry of a labeled one. If the binding has a hop count, the outgoing TTL is the larger of 0 and the incoming TTL minus the hop count; otherwise it is the larger of 0 and the incoming TTL minus one. If the result is zero the packet MUST NOT be sent as a labeled packet: it is treated as expired (possibly triggering an ICMP message), or forwarded unlabeled over the non-MPLS connection with TTL one less. These rules apply only to unicast packets.

Every ATM-LSR MUST also implement, as a configurable option, loop detection via path vectors (LDPV). A request carries a path vector of LSR addresses; an LSR that finds its own address in it concludes the request looped and acts as if the hop count exceeded MAXHOP. LSRs that support VC-merge SHOULD NOT include path vectors in downstream requests. The option detects loops faster, at a higher cost in overhead. Without it, the hop count mechanism detects loops.
sections.plainLanguage: The old machines cannot count down how much time a parcel has left, so the staff at the edge subtract the right number. A list of stops visited helps spot a parcel going round in circles.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The encapsulation and procedures do not interfere with authentication or encryption of network layer packets, such as IPSEC applied to IP datagrams. They do not protect against accidental or malicious alteration of MPLS labels, which could cause misforwarding, and they do not let a receiving LSR authenticate the transmitting LSR. Security considerations for label distribution are discussed in RFC 3036.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here stops someone from scribbling on a tag or proves who handed you a parcel, so those protections must come from elsewhere.
